content.title: About
content.content: Bacon and Tomato Dressing is a ready‑to‑use sauce blend that combines smoky bacon flavor with fresh tomato notes. It works well on salads, sandwiches, and pasta dishes, adding a rich, slightly sweet and subtly smoky taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dressing merges two classic flavors—bacon and tomatoes—commonly found in American cuisine.
Typical ingredients include real tomatoes, spices, bacon flavoring (or real bacon bits), and a touch of vinegar for balance.
Bacon can be present as actual meat or as a natural flavor extract, making some versions suitable for vegetarians when labeled accordingly.
The sauce is often used as a marinade for meat, fish, or vegetables before grilling or roasting.
Its thick consistency allows easy drizzling without excessive runoff.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Bacon contributes animal protein, which is essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes and bacon provide B6 and B12 vitamins that support normal metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes are a good source of lycopene, an antioxidant linked to heart health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of fats and carbohydrates offers a quick source of energy.

items.title: Flavor enhancement
items.content: Adding the dressing can make meals more palatable, encouraging a more varied diet.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The dressing may contain a notable amount of salt, which should be limited by people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Bacon adds saturated fats, which should be moderated in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to meat or specific additives should check the ingredient list carefully.

items.title: Preservatives and flavorings
items.content: Some versions may contain artificial preservatives that can cause sensitivity in certain consumers.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drizzle the dressing over salads, use it as a meat or vegetable marinade, toss with cooked pasta, or spread on sandwiches. For a lighter taste, thin it with a little olive oil or yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dressing refrigerated after opening, in a tightly sealed container, and consume within 7‑10 days. Prevent exposure to air to avoid fat oxidation. Discard if the smell changes or the color darkens.

beef-steak-ribeye-lean-only-eaten.title: Beef, steak, ribeye, lean only eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Ribeye steak is a cut from the beef rib section, known for its tenderness and rich beefy flavor. This version uses only the lean portion without visible fat, making it more diet‑friendly while retaining the characteristic taste and texture of the meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name ribeye comes from the eye‑shaped muscle in the rib area that gives the cut its distinctive marbling.
Lean ribeye is often favored in Asian cuisines where a clean meat flavor is prized.
Beef is a rich source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.
Traditionally, ribeye is grilled or pan‑seared to medium doneness to keep it juicy.
In the United States, ribeye ranks among the most popular steaks in steakhouses.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Lean ribeye provides about 22 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Heme iron in beef helps improve blood formation and prevents anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support immune function and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Lean steak contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Even lean cuts contain some saturated fat, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor harmful bacteria such as E. coli or salmonella.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef proteins.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Beef is rich in purines, which can exacerbate gout in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ribeye is best cooked over high heat—grill, cast‑iron skillet, or broiler. Aim for medium doneness to keep it juicy. Let the steak sit at room temperature for 20‑30 minutes before cooking and rest for 5‑10 minutes after cooking so the juices redistribute. Serve with vegetables, salads, or a light sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh steak in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or in an airtight container, and use within 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C in a vacuum‑sealed bag, where it retains quality for 6‑12 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Cottage cheese with gelatin dessert is a soft curd product that contains added gelatin, creating a light, jelly‑like texture. It is often enjoyed as a light dessert or snack, combining the creamy taste of cottage cheese with the airy feel of gelatin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottage cheese is a staple in Eastern European cuisine, and gelatin adds a fluffy dimension.
Gelatin is derived from collagen, usually sourced from animal bones and skin.
The dessert is typically served chilled, sometimes topped with fruit sauce or fresh berries.
In the Soviet era, similar desserts were homemade using gelatin sheets.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Cottage cheese provides high‑quality dairy protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Low in fat (when made with low‑fat cheese)
items.content: Low‑fat versions deliver nutrients without excess calories.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Gelatin may help improve gut lining health and aid digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cottage cheese contains B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy may react to the product.

items.title: Gelatin source
items.content: Gelatin is animal‑derived, making the dessert unsuitable for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some commercial versions add salt, which should be considered by those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cottage cheese with gelatin as a standalone dessert, add it to fruit salads, drizzle with honey or berry sauce, or cut into cubes for a light snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. Once opened, it is best consumed within 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or changes texture.

pizza-with-extra-meat-and-extra-vegetabl.title: Pizza with extra meat and extra vegetables, medium crust

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with extra meat and extra vegetables on a medium crust is a classic Italian pizza enriched with additional portions of meat (such as ham, sausage, or chicken) and a variety of vegetables (tomatoes, bell peppers, onions, mushrooms). The medium‑thick dough provides a balance between a crisp edge and a soft interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The meat‑and‑vegetable combo makes this pizza more filling and nutritionally dense.
Medium crust is typically baked at 220‑250 °C, yielding a golden‑brown crust.
Traditionally the pizza is served hot right out of the oven so the cheese stays stretchy.
Variations may include different cheeses such as mozzarella, parmesan, or cheddar.
Pizzas with extra toppings are often ordered in pizzerias as a “premium combo.”

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The added meat provides a substantial amount of high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables contribute vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium and fiber, supporting immunity and digestion.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: Carbohydrates from the dough, fats from the cheese, and protein from the meat give lasting satiety.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and bell peppers contain lycopene and vitamin C, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: Protein from meat combined with dough carbs aids muscle recovery after exercise.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Extra meat and cheese increase the calorie count, so portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Processed meats and some cheeses can be high in salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Large amounts of cheese and meat raise saturated fat intake, potentially affecting cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the pizza into serving pieces and enjoy it hot. Fresh basil or arugula added after baking enhances aroma. Optionally drizzle with hot sauce or olive oil for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore a crispy crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomatoes, scalloped (Scalloped Tomatoes) are a canned vegetable product made from whole tomatoes covered with a creamy sauce of butter, flour, milk, and seasonings, then baked until a golden crust forms. The product is commonly used as a side dish or an ingredient in casseroles, stews, and other recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scalloped tomatoes first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient way to preserve fresh tomatoes for winter.
The creamy sauce is typically made from milk, butter, and wheat flour, giving the dish a smooth texture.
Nutmeg is often added to the sauce to enhance the natural sweetness of the tomatoes.
Canning retains most of the vitamin C, though some is lost during the heat treatment.
Scalloped tomatoes are frequently served as a standalone side with roasted chicken, pork, or beef.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and C
items.content: Tomatoes provide vitamins A and C, essential for vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in tomatoes aids digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Creamy sauce adds calcium
items.content: The dairy component of the sauce supplies calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Low in fat when consumed in moderation
items.content: When eaten in reasonable portions, the product contains modest amounts of saturated fat, fitting into a balanced diet.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: The creamy sauce can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned versions often contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Added sugars in some recipes
items.content: Certain formulations may include added sugar, which is not recommended for diabetics.

items.title: Potential BPA in packaging
items.content: If the product is packaged in plastic, ensure it is BPA‑free to avoid possible health concerns.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Scalloped tomatoes can be served as a side with meat, fish, or poultry, mixed into casseroles, pasta, risotto, or used as a filling for pies. They reheat well in the microwave or on the stovetop, stirring to distribute the sauce evenly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened jar in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.
